original: A functor on the opposite category is written as $h_x(y)=\mathrm{Hom}(x,y)$, while the subsequent arrows use $\mathrm{Hom}(y,x)$.
correction: For the contravariant representable functor use $h_x(y)=\mathrm{Hom}(y,x)$. An arrow $f:y\to y'$ in the original category induces precomposition $\mathrm{Hom}(y',x)\to\mathrm{Hom}(y,x)$.
reason: Composition with $f$ reverses the source variable. The expression $\mathrm{Hom}(x,-)$ is instead covariant.

original: The proof of limit preservation describes a covariant representable functor as $x\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(x,z)$ and concludes that every Hom functor is continuous.
correction: The covariant representable functor preserving limits is $\mathrm{Hom}(z,-)$. The contravariant functor $\mathrm{Hom}(-,z)$ turns colimits in the original category into limits of sets.
reason: The displayed source and target variance disagree. Applying the universal property of a limit to maps from a fixed object gives the covariant assertion.

original: The Yoneda proof takes $\theta:z\to x$ and writes $\eta_x(\alpha)=F(\theta)(\alpha)$ for $\alpha\in F(z)$.
correction: For $h_z=\mathrm{Hom}(-,z)$ take $\theta:x\to z$ and write $\eta_x(\theta)=F(\theta)(\alpha)$, where $\alpha=\eta_z(1_z)\in F(z)$.
reason: The component $\eta_x$ accepts a morphism $x\to z$, while contravariance sends such a morphism to $F(z)\to F(x)$. This fixes both the arrow direction and the component's argument.

original: The universal map to an arbitrary module product is written as $\psi(n)=\sum_{i\in I}p_i(n)$.
correction: The universal map is $\psi(n)=(p_i(n))_{i\in I}\in\prod_{i\in I}M_i$.
reason: Its coordinates belong to different modules and can have infinite support. A tuple is defined in the product, whereas the displayed sum is generally undefined.

original: The Grothendieck-group remark defines $K_0(A)$ by identifying projectives that become isomorphic after adding possibly different free modules.
correction: The usual $K_0(A)$ is generated by isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective modules with relations $[P\oplus Q]=[P]+[Q]$. Quotienting by the subgroup generated by $[A]$ additionally forgets free summands and is a reduced construction.
reason: For a field $k$, usual $K_0(k)$ is $\mathbb Z$ by dimension, while the source's stable-free equivalence identifies every finite-dimensional vector space with zero.

original: The injective lifting equation is written as $q\circ\tilde\pi=\pi$, and a lemma claims an injection $M\to M^\wedge$.
correction: For an inclusion $q:M'\hookrightarrow M$, extension means $\tilde\pi\circ q=\pi$. For $M^\wedge=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(M,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$, the canonical injection is evaluation $M\hookrightarrow M^{\wedge\wedge}$, $m\mapsto(\chi\mapsto\chi(m))$.
reason: The first composition is not type-correct. Separation of points by characters proves injectivity into the double character group, not a canonical map into the single character group. The same corrections apply to the overlapping supplementary note supp02.

original: Dualizing $0\to U\to V\to W\to0$ is stated to yield $0\to U^\vee\to V^\vee\to W^\vee\to0$.
correction: For the stated finite free modules, dualization gives the exact sequence $0\to W^\vee\to V^\vee\to U^\vee\to0$.
reason: A dual map is defined by precomposition and therefore reverses arrows. Exactness here follows because the original sequence splits.

original: The inverse-limit exactness statement is written with arrows $0\leftarrow\varprojlim M'_i\leftarrow\varprojlim M_i\leftarrow\varprojlim M''_i$.
correction: For a compatible system of short exact sequences, left exactness is $0\to\varprojlim M'_i\to\varprojlim M_i\to\varprojlim M''_i$.
reason: The transition from each module to its inverse limit is covariant in maps of systems. Inverse limits preserve kernels, giving the displayed sequence with forward arrows; surjectivity at the final term is not automatic.

original: An example says that $R=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ for $n\ge2$ is not flat, without specifying any other base ring or module.
correction: As written, this example is false: $R$ is free of rank one over itself and hence flat. It is also a free, and therefore flat, $k$-module. A different module or ring map would have to be specified for a nonflatness example.
reason: The earlier example in the same section proves that every ring is flat as a module over itself. Polynomial monomials form a basis over $k$.

original: The tensor product of two supercommutative algebras is said to be supercommutative with the total grading, immediately after ordinary tensor-product multiplication.
correction: For the graded tensor product use $(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=(-1)^{|b||a'|}aa'\otimes bb'$ for homogeneous elements. This signed multiplication gives supercommutativity for the total grading.
reason: Without the sign, odd elements from different factors commute under ordinary tensor multiplication, whereas supercommutativity requires them to anticommute when 2 is nonzero.

original: The exterior algebra is defined by the relations $xy+yx=0$ and then identified with the quotient by all $z^2=0$ over an arbitrary commutative ring.
correction: Over an arbitrary commutative ring, define the exterior algebra by $z^2=0$ for all $z\in M$. These relations imply $xy+yx=0$; the converse requires an additional hypothesis such as 2 being invertible.
reason: In characteristic 2, the relation $xx+xx=0$ imposes no condition on $x^2$. For a rank-one module over $\mathbb F_2$, the anticommutativity quotient still has nonzero higher powers, unlike its exterior algebra.

original: The theorem labeled going up asserts that every prime of $A$ lifts along an arbitrary integral homomorphism $f:A\to B$.
correction: For an integral homomorphism, primes of $B$ lie over the primes of $A$ containing $\ker f$; every prime lifts when the map is an integral inclusion. This is the lying-over statement. Going up additionally extends compatible chains of prime ideals.
reason: The integral quotient map $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ has no prime lying over $(3)$. Every contraction must contain the kernel $(2)$.

original: The first elimination theorem claims that a single coefficient polynomial $R$ detects a nonzero common zero for any numbers of homogeneous equations and variables.
correction: In general the coefficient condition is a closed locus defined by an ideal of equations, rather than a single resultant polynomial. The classical single resultant applies under suitable hypotheses, including the standard case of as many homogeneous forms as variables.
reason: For the homogeneous equation $ax+by=0$ in two variables together with additional arbitrary forms, common-zero loci need not be hypersurfaces. More directly, two linear forms $ax$ and $bx$ in one variable have a nonzero common zero exactly when $a=b=0$, a codimension-two locus in the coefficient plane over an algebraically closed field.

original: The proof of $\sqrt I=\bigcap_{\mathfrak p\supseteq I}\mathfrak p$ starts from membership in every prime and concludes radical membership without supplying an argument.
correction: If $f^n\in I$, primality gives $f\in\mathfrak p$ for every prime containing $I$. Conversely, if $f\notin\sqrt I$, then $S=\{1,f,f^2,\ldots\}$ is disjoint from $I$. A maximal ideal in the nonzero ring $S^{-1}(A/I)$ contracts to a prime containing $I$ but not $f$.
reason: The easy inclusion runs from the radical to the intersection. Localization supplies the missing reverse inclusion by producing a separating prime.

original: A remark attributes a splitting of $0\to I_Y\to C(X)\to C(Y)\to0$ for every closed subset of a compact Hausdorff space to the Gelfand–Naimark theorem.
correction: For continuous real-valued functions, restriction is surjective by the Tietze extension theorem. A ring or algebra splitting does not follow in general and must not be asserted without further hypotheses.
reason: For $X=[0,1]$ and $Y=\{0,1\}$, a ring section would send the nontrivial idempotent $(1,0)\in C(Y)$ to a continuous idempotent on the connected interval with different endpoint values. Such a function cannot exist.

original: The supplementary Grothendieck-group subsection uses stable isomorphism after adding different free summands as its definition of $K_0$.
correction: Use the usual direct-sum Grothendieck group $K_0(A)$ and distinguish the quotient that forgets free summands. The overlapping main-lecture clarification in a2s12 applies here as well.
reason: Over a field, ordinary $K_0$ records dimension, whereas the source's stable-free equivalence identifies all finite-dimensional vector spaces.

original: The supplementary injective criterion writes $q\circ\tilde\pi=\pi$ and its character-group lemma states $M\to M^\wedge$.
correction: The extension equation is $\tilde\pi\circ q=\pi$. The canonical injective evaluation map has target the double character group $M^{\wedge\wedge}$.
reason: Composition must first include the submodule and then apply its extended map. Characters separate points and therefore prove injectivity of evaluation into the double dual, as explained for a2s13.

original: The quadratic-integer example assigns $\mathbb Z[\sqrt d]$ to $d\equiv1\pmod4$ and $\mathbb Z[(1+\sqrt d)/2]$ to $d\equiv2,3\pmod4$.
correction: For a square-free integer $d$, the ring of integers of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$ is $\mathbb Z[(1+\sqrt d)/2]$ when $d\equiv1\pmod4$, and $\mathbb Z[\sqrt d]$ when $d\equiv2,3\pmod4$.
reason: The cases are reversed. The element $(1+\sqrt d)/2$ has monic polynomial $T^2-T+(1-d)/4$, whose constant term is integral exactly in the first congruence case.

original: The proof of Fermat's sum-of-two-squares theorem calls $\mathbb Q(i)$ a principal ideal domain before using prime-ideal factorization.
correction: The relevant principal ideal domain is the Gaussian integer ring $\mathbb Z[i]$, which is Euclidean for the norm $a+bi\mapsto a^2+b^2$.
reason: The ideals and their generators in the argument belong to the ring of integers $\mathbb Z[i]$. The field $\mathbb Q(i)$ has only the zero and unit ideals, so its ideal theory cannot provide the displayed factorization of $(p)$.
